summary: VNVSpec is an open-source Python framework that stores requirements, hazards, contracts and evidence as typed objects in YAML, TOML or Python. It adds a lexical requirement-quality checker (8 INCOSE GtWR rules), standards clause registries and 116 curated catalog requirements, a cycle-free traceability graph built from requirement-ID markers in tests, evidence ingestion from pytest and JUnit XML (so Java and JS runners work), and verdict roll-up with audit exports. All evaluation is self-application: its own 36-requirement spec verified by 449 tests, synthetic runtime scaling to 10,000 requirements, about 0.8 ms per-test plugin overhead, and seeded defects in which the checker catches escape clauses and missing criteria (36/36) but no packed conditions (0/36).

claims.claim: The specification language is expressive enough for a nontrivial system, and continuous self-assessment catches real defects
claims.evidence: §IV-C2: 36 requirements across 12 blocking / 17 high / 7 medium, verified by 449 tests under a 95% branch-coverage gate; two anecdotal regressions caught. No external project and no comparison.

claims.claim: Core operations scale linearly and can handle up to 10,000 requirements
claims.evidence: Table II: synthetic specs of 10-10,000 requirements on a 2-core CI machine, medians of 5 runs (3 for the largest); quality check 0.35 s and trace graph 0.12 s at 10k; YAML load dominates (10.2 s). Runtime only.

claims.claim: Integration overhead is small (~0.8 ms per test; JUnit ingestion ~11,000 cases/s)
claims.evidence: §IV-C4: 400 no-op tests 0.90 s -> 1.23 s with plugin; a 5,000-case JUnit XML file with 4% failures ingested in 0.46 s with all verdicts recovered. Synthetic but measures what it claims.

claims.claim: The quality checker detects seeded requirement defects
claims.evidence: Table III: escape clauses 36/36, removed acceptance criteria 36/36, vague terms 17/36 (masked when the original already triggers the rule), packed second conditions 0/36. Operators were chosen by the authors to align with the checker's own rule classes; negative results reported openly.

claims.claim: The framework extends to testing black-box AI models and AI coding agents
claims.evidence: §IV-A and §VI describe an envisioned agent protocol; the authors state that orchestrating agents is left to future work. Model adapters exist, but no agent is evaluated.

patterns.note: Requirement IDs in pytest markers or JUnit test titles become 'verifies' edges in an enforced DAG. Marker references are validated against the spec at collection time, unknown IDs produce warnings, and requirements with no linked test become 'inconclusive' rather than passing. No comparison with Doorstop, Sphinx-needs or manual matrices, and no measurement of link correctness or authoring effort on a real project (acknowledged in §VI).

Requirements carry a verification method, metric and acceptance criteria; the lexical gate catches escape clauses and missing criteria (36/36) but misses compound requirements (0/36), and inspects phrasing, not correctness. No comparison with human review.
Standards clause registries and version-pinned best-practice catalogs (116 requirements, 71% mapped to clauses) shipped as importable machine-readable data; usefulness not evaluated.
Proposes that coding agents state tier-1 requirements and decompositions as typed objects reviewed by the quality gate and humans; not built or tested.

methodology.sample: One project (VNVSpec itself: 36 requirements, 449 tests); synthetic specs of 10-10,000 requirements; 400 no-op tests; one 5,000-case JUnit file; 144 mutants (36 x 4 operators)
methodology.baselines: None (no comparison with Doorstop, Sphinx-needs, BDD/Cucumber or manual traceability)
methodology.models: None (no LLM in the evaluated system)
methodology.variance: Medians of 5 runs (3 for largest sizes); no spread reported
methodology.languages: Python core; JUnit XML route demonstrated with Jest; Java claimed via JUnit XML but not demonstrated

standards.artifacts: Code, full test suite, catalogs and benchmark scripts on GitHub; packages on PyPI

biases.detail: All evaluation by the authors, on the framework itself, on one machine, with seeded-defect operators of their choosing (stated in §VI).
Runtime and overhead measurements do not address the usefulness claims (traceability that survives in practice, audit readiness, authoring effort), as the authors acknowledge.
A single 36-requirement specification is the only real-world use.
Core and native plugin are Python; other ecosystems are covered only through JUnit XML ingestion, with a Jest example.

verdict_reason: A clear, released tool whose cost and scaling claims are measured and whose quality-checker limits are reported honestly. There is no evidence that it improves traceability, effort or outcomes versus any alternative, and the AI-agent extension is only proposed.
applicability: A concrete, deterministic pattern for the team's spec-driven rollout: requirement IDs in JUnit test names or annotations, JUnit XML ingestion into a requirement-to-test DAG, 'no linked test means inconclusive, not pass', and distinct CI exit codes per verdict. This fits qr's verify/commit/reject stance and works across 4 Java repos without changing test runners. The lexical checker is a cheap pre-spec filter for vague words and missing acceptance criteria, but it misses compound requirements entirely, so it cannot replace a clarification step with people or an agent. The catalogs are Python/ML/FastAPI-specific, so a healthcare-content team would write its own (content schema, accessibility, delivery contracts). The paper says nothing about discovery or onboarding, and nothing shows the approach reduces effort.
